readerTitle: The yogurt plant nobody wanted: how Chobani got its start
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Chobani, Kraft의 South Edmeston 공장) + 가상 적용 (냉난방 수리업체 인수)
insight: 같은 자산도 주인에 따라 가치가 다르다. 큰 회사가 버리는 자산은 그 회사의 쓰임새 기준으로 값이 매겨지므로, 다른 쓰임새를 가진 사람에게는 가장 싼 출발점이 될 수 있다.
misconception: 큰 회사가 닫는 공장이나 사업은 가치가 없어서 버려지는 것이다. 창업은 처음부터 새로 짓는 것이 가장 안전하다.

sources.text: Hamdi Ulukaya, TED talk "The anti-CEO playbook" (2019): 우편 광고로 공장 매물을 본 일, 공장 인수 결정
Chobani 공식 회사 연혁 (2005년 South Edmeston 공장 인수, 2007년 첫 출하)
U.S. Small Business Administration 관련 자료 및 언론 보도 (SBA 보증 대출로 인수 자금 마련)
Forbes, Inc., The New York Times 등 2012~2013년 Chobani 창업 과정 보도 (전 Kraft 직원 채용, 터키 출신 요구르트 전문가 영입, 약 5년 만의 연 매출 10억 달러)

factChecks.note: 공장 인수 시점(2005년), 위치(뉴욕주 South Edmeston), 이전 소유주(Kraft)를 Chobani 공식 연혁으로 확인하세요.
인수 가격은 보도마다 다르게 나옵니다(100만 달러 미만 등). 카드에는 구체적 금액을 넣지 않고 'far less than building a new plant'로만 적었습니다.
재고용한 전 Kraft 직원 수는 '5명'으로 자주 보도되지만, 카드에는 'a handful'로 적었습니다. 요구르트 전문가(Mustafa Dogan) 영입도 확인 필요.
첫 출하 2007년, 레시피 개발 약 2년, 출시 약 5년 만에 연 매출 10억 달러 돌파라는 수치를 1차 보도로 확인하세요.
Ulukaya가 기존에 페타 치즈 사업을 했다는 내용, SBA 보증 대출 사용 여부를 확인하세요.

cards.title: The yogurt plant nobody wanted
body: In 2005, Hamdi Ulukaya, a Turkish immigrant running a small feta cheese business in upstate New York, saw a real estate flyer in his mail. Kraft was selling an old yogurt plant nearby.
He had never made yogurt at scale. The plant was closing because it didn't fit the plans of one of the biggest food companies in the world.

image.label: An old empty factory with a for-sale sign
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 시골 언덕 위 오래된 낮은 공장 건물, 정문에 'FOR SALE' 표지판. 앞에 우편 전단 한 장이 바람에 날림. 실제 기업 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Would you buy the plant?
body: You run a small cheese business. A giant company is closing a yogurt factory near you. It comes with equipment, a building and a region full of dairy farms. You have no yogurt brand and no big customers.

options.text: Buy it, using a loan, and learn to make yogurt there
options.feedback: You get a whole factory for far less than building one, but you take on debt before you have a single customer.

options.text: Pass. If Kraft couldn't make it work, neither can you
options.feedback: You avoid the debt and the risk, but you assume the plant failed, when it may only have failed to fit Kraft.

options.text: Pay another factory to make a small test batch first
options.feedback: You learn cheaply whether people want your yogurt, but the plant may be sold to someone else while you test.

choice.afterReveal: Ulukaya bought it. The real question is why a plant one giant didn't want could be worth so much to him.

cards.title: From empty plant to market leader.
body: He bought the plant with a loan for far less than building a new one would cost. He hired a handful of its former workers and brought in a yogurt expert from Turkey. Then they spent about two years perfecting a thick, strained Greek-style yogurt before selling a single cup.

breakdown.label: Buys the plant
breakdown.detail: An old Kraft factory in South Edmeston, New York

breakdown.label: First cups ship
breakdown.detail: After roughly two years on the recipe

breakdown.label: $1 billion in yearly sales
breakdown.detail: Chobani becomes a leading US yogurt brand

cards.title: An asset is worth what it can do *for you*.
body: **The same asset has different value to different owners.** To Kraft, the plant was a small piece of a huge network that no longer fit its plans. Its price reflected that.

To Ulukaya, it was everything he needed in one place: machines, trained people and fresh milk nearby. A seller prices an asset for its old use. A buyer with a different plan can get far more out of it.

image.label: One factory seen through two different lenses
image.brief: 같은 공장 그림을 좌우로 나눔. 왼쪽은 큰 회사 지도 위 작은 점 하나로 보이며 'Doesn't fit our plan' 라벨. 오른쪽은 같은 공장이 크게 보이며 'Machines', 'Skilled people', 'Milk nearby' 라벨. 로고 없음.

cards.title: What came with the building.
body: The plant saved Ulukaya more than construction costs. It came with things that are slow to build from scratch:
list: **People** who knew how to run it
**Time**, spent on the recipe instead of on building
cards.callout: He put the saved years into the product, the part a factory can't supply.

cards.title: Look for assets that left someone's plan.
body: The pattern shows up everywhere. A closed restaurant leaves a fitted kitchen that a new café can open in within weeks. A retiring accountant leaves a client list and a trained assistant. A chain shrinking its stores leaves good locations behind.
In each case, the seller leaves for its own reasons. Your job is to see what the asset can do in your plan, not theirs.
cards.softwareNote: When a larger company shuts down a product or a side tool, its code, domain or user base can sometimes be bought cheaply. It was a distraction for them and can be a running start for a small team.

cards.title: Cheap is not the same as ready.
body: First, ask **why the seller is leaving**. Kraft left for reasons of its own strategy. If a seller leaves because demand is dying or the location is bad, the low price is a warning, not a gift.
Second, an asset doesn't earn money by itself. Ulukaya paid a loan for about two years before selling anything. Buying a start means you need enough cash to survive until the product is good.

cards.title: Now it's a home repair business.
body: You run a small plumbing company. A local heating and air-conditioning repair owner is retiring. He offers his vans, tools and 300 yearly maintenance contracts at a low price. His two technicians might stay.

options.text: Buy everything now. A price this low won't come again
options.feedback: You might get a bargain, but you skip asking whether the contracts renew and the technicians stay, which is where the real value is.

options.text: Check why he's selling, talk to the technicians and a few contract customers, then buy what fits your plan
options.feedback: You spend a few weeks, but you learn whether he's leaving for personal reasons or because the business is fading.

options.text: Pass and build your own heating service from scratch
options.feedback: You avoid inherited problems, but you give up years of customers, skills and equipment that could have come ready-made.

cards.title: Someone else's exit can be your cheapest start.
body: Assets are priced for the seller's plan. If yours is different, ask what the asset can do for you, why they're leaving, and how long until it earns.
**Try it today:** list one asset near your business that someone is giving up: a space, equipment, a client list. Write down what it could do in your plan.
